paper_title: GTAGym: Real AAA Game Tasks Environment for Evaluation and Reinforcement Learning

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: AAA games offer a rich testbed for evaluating agent perception, reasoning, and control. However, evaluating whether agents can complete tasks in AAA games is challenging and often human-annotated because task outcomes are often difficult to verify automatically, let alone applying it for Reinforcement Learning (RL). We introduce GTAGym, an environment and framework for evaluation and RL on GTA V tasks. Its evaluation benchmark, GTAVBench, derived from GTA V main-story missions, contains 103 online tasks reconstructed across nine task families, alongside 47 image-based shooting and sniping tasks using GTA V imagery. A web server provides access to the online environment and evaluation interface, supporting parallel testing through screenshots and keyboard-mouse actions with automatic engine-state outcome checks. We evaluate six frontier LLMs on GTAVBench with textual task instructions and on its GTAVBench-AGI branch, where instructions appear only in the first screenshot and a harness automatically compresses interaction history. The best configuration achieves 70.9% overall accuracy in GTAVBench-AGI, yet aerial navigation, evasion and interception remain difficult. GTAGym also provides a scalable generator that samples task parameters within user-specified ranges and option sets under fixed templates, creating batches of 3D and image-based shooting environments for RL with automatic reward and termination signals. LoRA RL of Qwen3.8-27B on generated on-foot navigation tasks improves the in-domain performance and transfers to out-of-domain task categories, and native GTA V tasks from 15% to 23%.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Building agents that can perceive, reason, and act in real-world environments as flexibly as humans is an ultimate goal of artificial general intelligence (AGI) [5]. Sim-to-real transfer is common approach to developing real-world agent capabilities: models are trained in simulation and then transferred to physical environments [15, 20]. Among simulated environments, AAA open-world games offer rich testbed: navigation, vehicle control, and interactions with moving characters require spatial understanding, temporal reasoning, and action execution [1, 18]. Vision-language models are increasingly deployed as agents that translate visual observations and natural-language goals into actions [18, 22]. Evaluating these agents requires measuring whether their actions achieve task goals over an extended interaction. Existing work follows three broad directions: verifiable tasks in sandbox and purpose-built games [5, 8, 13], Corresponding authors: wangyuxin@sii.edu.cn, xpqiu@sii.edu.cn. 1 agents that act in commercial 3D worlds [1, 18, 19], and benchmarks that assess gameplay through visual trajectories or offline questions [21, 25, 27]. These directions advance task verification, realistic interaction, and broad coverage, respectively. Bringing them together requires an environment that preserves objectives from real AAA missions, verifies outcomes automatically, and generates new executable tasks for training. Table 1 compares these features across representative benchmarks. We introduce GTAGym, an environment and framework that decomposes main-story missions from GTA [16] into reusable tasks defined by their goals, interaction stages, completion constraints, and dynamic behaviors. Its evaluation benchmark, GTAVBench, contains 103 online tasks across nine families of navigation, vehicle control, and dynamic interaction, plus 47 image-based shooting and sniping tasks using GTA imagery. GTAVBench supplies textual task instructions; its GTAVBench-AGI branch presents them only in the first screenshot, as in-game objectives, and uses harness with automatic context compression. web server exposes shared screenshot-and-action interface for parallel evaluation, with built-in evaluators checking online outcomes from engine states. The same framework samples task parameters within user-defined ranges to generate batches of RL environments with automatic reward and termination signals. Figure 1 summarizes GTAVBench-AGI performance with the Codex harness across the eleven evaluation categories. Figure 1 Accuracy (%) of six models with the Codex harness on GTAVBench-AGI, across eleven task categories. Outer arcs group tasks into Navigation, Interaction, and Gun Use. Our contributions are: We provide GTAGym, an environment for parallel evaluation of tasks derived from real AAA gameplay. Built-in evaluators determine task outcomes directly from engine states, removing the need for manual outcome judgments and bringing the programmatic task verification available in Minecraft platforms such as MineDojo [5] to tasks derived from GTA missions. We construct GTAVBench from GTA main-story missions and introduce its GTAVBench-AGI branch. The former supplies textual task instructions, while the latter presents goals in the initial game image and uses harness with automatic context compression. The results reveal persistent weaknesses in completing these mission-derived tasks, particularly in aerial control, evasion and interception. 2 We equip GTAGym with scalable, template-based generator of reinforcement-learning task environments. Each template fixes the scene and task rules while exposing sampling parameters such as movement mode, route length, turn count, and actor speed. Users restrict their ranges or candidate sets to generate 3D and image-based shooting environments in batches, with automatic reward and termination signals to support RL training of exploration, control, and aiming skills.

sections.title: 2.1 Foundation-Model Agents for Video Games
sections.content: Foundation models combine visual perception, instruction following, and action selection to operate in commercial games. Cradle uses screenshots and keyboardmouse control with planning, memory, and reflection modules, demonstrating main-story progression in Red Dead Redemption 2 [18]. SIMA learns instruction-following behavior across simulated 3D worlds, using ground-truth checks in research environments and OCR or human judgments in commercial games [1]; SIMA 2 extends this direction with higher-level reasoning and self-improvement [2]. Lumine trains an end-to-end vision-language policy for keyboardmouse control in open worlds and uses human evaluation for its task benchmark [19]. OctoGTA instruments GTA through scripting plugins, exposing game entities and programmatic action functions for visually guided task execution [23]. GTAGym instead reconstructs mission-derived tasks with engine-state evaluators and shared screenshot-and-action interface, supporting parallel evaluation and RL environment generation.

sections.title: 2.2 Multimodal Game Benchmarks
sections.content: Games have long served as testbeds for learning and evaluating interactive agents. Procgen studies RL generalization through procedurally generated levels [3], while MineDojo provides configurable Minecraft tasks and rewards for open-ended learning [5]. More recent benchmarks evaluate foundation-model agents across diverse games: lmgame-Bench studies perception, memory, and reasoning [7], Orak examines agent modules and fine-tuning across commercial games [14], and VideoGameBench measures visual gameplay progress and the effects of inference latency [25]. Specialized benchmarks such as LongPuzzleBench further test long-horizon decision-making in visual puzzles [26]. Recent work also develops evaluation protocols for richer game environments. GameWorld provides state-verifiable browser tasks and parallel execution [13], while OmniGameArena introduces custom UE5 games for solo, competitive, and cooperative evaluation [8]. For commercial AAA games, GameVerse scores progress through VLM-based milestone matching and studies improvement from video reflection [27]; GameHorizon-Bench evaluates AAA gameplay offline, with its verifiable online track implemented in Minecraft [21]. Our work brings objectives extracted from GTA main-story missions into an environment with built-in outcome checks, parallel web execution, and parameterized RL instance generation. Table 1 compares these features with prior benchmarks.

sections.title:
3.2 Task Construction
Task extraction and specification. We manually decompose 75 GTA V main-story missions into subtasks based
on collected walkthrough videos, each corresponding to a distinct stage in a mission. For each subtask, we
specify the goal, required interaction order, completion constraints, and entity behaviors used to reconstruct
it in our environment. These annotations and source game images support the construction of 150 benchmark
tasks across eleven categories.
sections.content: Online scenario reconstruction. We build the 3D environment using Babylon.js and implement task controllers that expose task-specific states. Task specifications configure initial positions, destinations, vehicles, interaction objects, and moving actors. For navigation tasks, we manually trace paths on the source minimap and seek routes with comparable turn counts in the available city geometry. We add climbing surfaces and landing areas where required by the task. Dynamic-interaction tasks use predefined NPC behaviors and mechanics such as collision-induced slowdown. The resulting scenarios preserve the selected goals, interaction dependencies, and movement constraints while adapting their spatial layout to the evaluation environment. Image-based task construction. Shooting and sniping use parallel construction process based on source game imagery. For shooting, we select gameplay frames and associate targets with annotated hit regions. For sniping, we capture images directly in GTA to construct distinct unscoped and scoped views with magnification-dependent rendering. Template instantiation and verification. We instantiate each subtask description as scenario template with an initial state, an instruction, task budget, and executable success and failure predicates. The goal specifies the destination, target, or interaction outcome; stage transitions specify the required order of interactions. Completion predicates check movement mode, height or depth, target distance, and interaction events according to the task. For following and pursuit, target controller executes predefined route that the agent must track through visual observations. 3.3 Evaluation
Shared interaction interface. GTAVBench and GTAVBench-AGI use the same task instances, action interface,
and scoring rules, differing in instruction presentation and context management. Both branches follow a
closed-loop screenshot–action protocol with keyboard–mouse control. By default, online 3D simulation pauses
during inference and advances during action execution. The agent specifies a hold duration 𝑑 ∈ (0, 𝑑max] for
each key, with 𝑑max = 1 second. Keys execute concurrently, and the turn duration is the longest scheduled
hold. Section 5.4 examines alternative duration limits and evaluation without inference-time pausing. The
image-based track uses the same action schema with its aiming interface. Complete trajectories are recorded
for analysis. The action space is specified in Appendix A.3.
sections.content: GTAVBench. Following screenshot-based computer-use evaluation [22], agents use fixed system prompt, textual task instruction, and screenshotreply history to generate JSON actions, which an adapter validates and executes. Online history is capped at ten pairs; exceeding the cap drops the oldest five while preserving the instruction. Image-based tasks retain the full history. See Appendix for prompt and history details. GTAVBench-AGI. We introduce GTAVBench-AGI as separate harness-based evaluation branch of GTAVBench. The task instruction appears only within the first screenshot, presenting the objective through the game view as in real gameplay. The agent must read the goal from the image and act through the same keyboardmouse interface. As interaction history grows, the Codex harness automatically compresses the context supplied to 5 the model [10]. Scoring. Episodes terminate upon task success, task failure, or exhaustion of an applicable turn or game-time budget. We report category-level accuracy and overall accuracy micro-averaged over 150 tasks. Task-specific outcome conditions are detailed in Appendix A.2; model configurations are specified in Section 4.

Parameter definitions, sampling domains, and template-specific settings are provided in Appendix B. Batch generation for RL. The rule-based generator in GTAGym samples configurations subject to the users bounds and the templates feasibility constraints. For example, driving template can restrict route length to [200, 500] meters and turn count to {2, 3, 4, 5}. These constraints jointly determine eligible routes; the generator rejects incompatible configurations and reports when no feasible instance can be found. It constructs the full route and initial state from the accepted values, then saves the resolved configuration and seed for reuse. Instances share the screenshotaction interface and use task outcomes as sparse rewards, with success and failure ending an episode and budget exhaustion recorded as truncation. The evaluator uses engine-state predicates for 3D tasks and target-hit checks for image-based tasks. Repeated sampling generates batches of RL environments within the requested parameter ranges.

sections.title: 4.1 Models and Baselines
sections.content: We evaluate six models on GTAVBench under the conventional GUI protocol: GPT-6-Astra [12], GPT-6.1Sol [11], DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 [4], GLM-5.3-Flash [24], Kimi-K3 [9], and Qwen3.8-27B. We additionally evaluate the GTAVBench-AGI branch using the Codex harness [10] under the protocol in Section 3.3. Additional model configurations are detailed in Appendix A.4. Navigation and interaction tasks allow up to 300 interaction rounds, while gun-use tasks allow up to 20. The human baseline evaluation protocol is described in Appendix A.5.

sections.title: 4.3 Reinforcement Learning
sections.content: We study whether reinforcement learning with low-rank adaptation (LoRA) [6] on generated on-foot environments improves task completion and transfers to other categories. Training environment generation. Using the generator in Section 3.4, we create 50 on-foot navigation instances, matching the benchmark categorys joint route-length and turn-count distribution and adding destination landmarks to some instances. The generated routes are spatially separated from the benchmarks on-foot routes; all benchmark tasks remain excluded from training. Generation and optimization details are provided in Appendix B.1. sections.title: 5 Analysis
sections.content: We analyze failure modes, error recovery, harness trade-offs, and evaluation settings.

sections.title: 5.1 Failure Mode Analysis
sections.content: Trajectory inspection reveals four recurring failure mechanisms. We contrast road-navigation behavior across models, then examine dynamic-control failures that persist even in frontier models. Table 11 in the appendix provides paired observations and executed actions for all four mechanisms. Mistimed steering. In road navigation, non-GPT models sometimes recognize an upcoming turn on the minimap but initiate steering too late or hold it too long for the current speed, overshooting the road. GPT models more effectively translate these cues into early braking and smaller heading corrections. Late descent correction. In aerial navigation, reaching the runway does not ensure safe landing. In the illustrated GPT trajectory, reducing throttle fails to arrest rapid descent; pitch correction follows too late to 8 Figure 4 Accuracy (%) before and after LoRA RL. Green marks the ID category (on-foot navigation), yellow marks OOD categories, and the purple Real Game axis aggregates 100 native GTA tasks. prevent crash. Coordinating attitude, speed, and descent remains difficult even when the destination is correctly identified. Failure to sustain blocking. In interception, slowing the target through collision is only an intermediate step. The agent continues accelerating after impact and loses contact instead of braking to hold blocking position, allowing the target to resume its route. Wall entrapment. In evasion, the agent continues applying forward throttle and steering against wall after hitting building, producing no displacement before eventually reversing. Such delays interrupt escape progress. Together, these cases expose difficulty anticipating motion and switching control strategies as the vehicle, target, or obstacle relationship changes.

sections.title: 5.2 Error Recovery Across Models
sections.content: To study the recovery ability of different models, we manually identify and annotate the first task-relevant error in each trajectory. We group first errors into four capability categories: Perception, Planning, Calibration, and Regulation. Across 900 trajectories from six models, our analysis includes 565 with an identified and categorized first error. Figure 5 shows that Calibration and Regulation dominate, together accounting for 63.2% of assigned first errors. This concentration suggests bottleneck in closed-loop control: calibrating action direction, magnitude, and duration, and adjusting maneuvers as motion and target states change. We then examine whether the agent subsequently recovers. Figure 6 shows that GPT models recover more reliably: Astra and Sol restore task progress within ten subsequent decisions in 65.7% and 49.3% of categorized first-error cases, compared with 21.6%25.6% for the other models. In road-navigation trajectories, GPT models correct off-road deviations and rejoin the intended route, resuming progress after local control errors.

sections.title: 5.3 Harness Trade-offs
sections.content: We study the instruction-presentation and context-management differences between GTAVBench and GTAVBench-AGI. Compared with the JSON runners ten-image window, the Codex harness preserves longer 9 Figure 5 First-error incidence in GTAVBench, as percentage of all 150 tasks per model. Figure 6 Recovery within ten decisions, as percentage of categorized first-error cases for each model and capability. histories and uses textual summaries to maintain continuity. This provides memory of attempted strategies, explored rooms, and interaction feedback, helping agents revise their plans and avoid repeated ineffective actions. In motorcycle interception, GPT-6-Astra recalls blocked approach and changes its maneuver before re-engaging; in indoor navigation, DeepSeek-Flash retains explored rooms and unsuccessful door interactions to guide further search. However, longer histories and compression can also preserve mistaken interpretations and weaken goal adherence. Kimi-K3 initially identifies rooftop objective correctly but, after compression, substitutes driving objective and later drops the original goal from its summary. GLM-5.3-Flash similarly carries reversed minimap-marker identities into subsequent decisions. These cases illustrate trajectory drift and goal loss around context handoffs.

sections.title: 5.4 Effects of Evaluation Settings
sections.content: We examine how the timing settings of the online 3D evaluation protocol affect task completion. Both ablations use GPT-6.1-Sol with the Codex harness on the 103 online 3D tasks in GTAVBench-AGI. Figure 7 compares the four distinct settings across the two ablations. Maximum action duration. We compare three values of 𝑑max: 0.5 s, 1 (default), and 2 s. The agent chooses each keys duration within (0, 𝑑max]; simulation pauses during inference in all three conditions. Relative to the 1 baseline (62.1%), reducing the cap to 0.5 raises overall accuracy to 66.3%, while increasing it to 2 lowers accuracy to 60.5%. Figure 7 shows the largest gains in following and interception, where shorter actions provide more frequent visual feedback. The tradeoff is more interaction and longer cumulative context: reducing the cap from 1 to 0.5 increases mean rounds from 62.6 to 121.2, input tokens from 4.32M to 11.20M, and output tokens from 4.27k to 7.66k. The mean maximum duration selected within an action increases with the allowed cap: 0.494, 0.916, and 1.468 s. At the 2 cap, 66.6% of actions exceed 1 s, although shorter inputs remain available. This suggests that model does not reliably choose appropriate action durations under our interface. Evaluation without pausing. With 𝑑max = 1 second, we let the simulation continue during model inference, releasing each key after its specified duration. Without pausing, overall accuracy drops by 22.3 percentage points to 39.8%. Following, interception, and police evasion fall to zero success, while on-foot and indoor navigation retain 100% accuracy and vertical navigation remains at 93.3% (Figure 7). This contrast points to inference latency as bottleneck for dynamic interaction: after short action ends, the environment continues evolving while the agent waits for its next decision. Targets can move beyond following range or reach their destinations, and police can capture the player before another corrective action is available. Tasks that tolerate waiting remain more tractable. Thus, real-time performance depends on whether the inference-and-action cycle is fast enough for the tasks response window. 10 Figure 7 Accuracy (%) of GPT-6.1-Sol with Codex across nine 3D task categories under four action-duration and inference-time pausing settings.

sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: We presented GTAGym, web-server-based environment and framework for evaluation and RL on tasks derived from GTA main-story missions. GTAVBench provides text-instructed evaluation, while its GTAVBench-AGI branch presents task goals only in the first screenshot and uses harness with automatic context compression. Both support parallel task execution and automatic outcome verification through unified interface. Experiments show that current agents remain limited in aerial control, evasion and interception. The environment generator in GTAGym complements GTAVBench by sampling numeric and categorical parameters within user-defined bounds under fixed templates, creating 3D and image-based shooting tasks with reward and termination signals for RL training. LoRA RL on generated on-foot navigation tasks improves Qwen3.8-27Bs task completion, with gains extending to unseen task categories and native GTA missions. Together, these components provide basis for evaluating and improving agents on tasks derived from real AAA gameplay.

sections.content: A.1 Task Categories and Mission Requirements Table 3 summarizes the eleven task categories and their mission requirements. Category Online 3D track: Navigation Road Aerial Aquatic Indoor On-Foot Vertical Online 3D track: Interaction Following Interception Evasion Image-based track: Gun Use Shooting Sniping Mission requirements Reach destination in road vehicle Takeoff, aerial objectives, and landing Depth, boarding, and shore-arrival objectives Reach interior goals and interact with doors or objects Reach destination on foot Reach target height using stairs or climbing Maintain proximity until the target arrives Stop or disable moving target Avoid detection and capture for required duration Locate and hit target in gameplay imagery Use scope and zoom to hit target or clear all specified targets Table 3 Task categories and the mission requirements implemented in the benchmark. Each category groups objectives with shared interaction and completion requirements. A.2 Task-Specific Outcome Conditions The evaluator determines completion from engine states and task events for online tasks, and from annotated hit regions for image-based tasks. Success is binary: incomplete route progress, unfinished interactions, and partially cleared target sets receive no partial credit. Both evaluation branches use the same predicates; an agents declaration of completion cannot substitute for satisfying them. Road and On-Foot. The agent must enter the destination region using the required movement mode: driving for road tasks and walking for on-foot tasks. Default horizontal tolerances are 24 and 3 m, respectively, with smaller task-specific regions for precise destinations. Arrival tests include the segment traversed between consecutive physics updates, so fast vehicle crossing the region is not missed between frames. Walking arrivals require ground support and cannot be triggered during jump or traversal animation. The displayed route and intermediate turns guide navigation without imposing mandatory checkpoints; physically feasible shortcuts are allowed. Vehicle-acquisition variants additionally require the agent to find and enter vehicle. Their ground-truth reference sequence includes the initial walking and boarding stages. Driving into deep water initiates irreversible sinking and prevents arrival success. Vertical and Indoor. These templates add height and interaction requirements to arrival. For example, the pickup-to-rooftop task requires grounded walking agent within 1 of the goal and 0.15 of the roof height; the ladder-to-rooftop task uses 1.1 horizontally and 0.35 vertically. Passing beneath an elevated goal does not complete it. Interior exits can use an oriented passage region instead of small circular goal, and the agent must reach the correct floor. Required interactions are checked through explicit mission state: the bank task requires pressing within 1.5 of the cash interaction point, opening the exit shutter, and leaving the building. The cover task requires pressing between the cover and the rear wall, within 0.85 of its interaction point, and completing the crouched pose. Other interiors can require an outward-and-return sequence before the final exit becomes valid. Following. The target follows its configured route while the evaluator checks the agenttarget distance throughout the episode. The maximum horizontal separation is 20 on foot and 200 in road vehicles. 14 Exceeding the applicable threshold causes immediate failure, whether the agent falls behind or moves too far ahead. Success occurs only after the target reaches its destination and the agent remains in the required movement state. Thus the agent must sustain following throughout the NPCs traversal. Returning within range after violation does not reverse terminal failure. Interception. For ordinary vehicle targets, the agent must establish frontal collision contact and continue blocking the target. Success requires the targets speed to remain at or below 3 m/s for 1.5 while the agent remains ahead, with collision gap below 2.5 and its own speed at or below 4 m/s. Braking from collision is integrated over time; naturally slow corner does not satisfy the interception condition. Motorcycle targets instead require three distinct knockdowns, each caused by an impact with at least 2 m/s closing speed. Further hits count only after recovery and separation; the third knockdown completes after the visible fall is complete and the motorcycle slows to at most 1 m/s. companion-recovery variant uses separate predicate: the agent must align alongside the moving truck and complete the companion transfer. For these tasks, the target reaching its endpoint before completion causes failure, including ties within physics update. Evasion. Evasion has no destination or prescribed route. Evasion has fixed maximum duration of 180 simulated seconds. The agent succeeds by remaining outside every pursuers scanning sector for sixty consecutive simulated seconds within this limit. Each sector has 12 radius and total angle of 90. Any exposure resets the undetected timer; three continuous seconds inside the union of scanning sectors causes capture. Leaving all sectors resets the capture timer. Pursuers and their visible minimap sectors use the same sensing geometry. Aquatic. Completion depends on the water-task subtype. Swimming goals use 3 horizontal tolerance and 0.8 depth tolerance; the submerged-entry task, for example, requires depth of 6 0.8 m. Boat-arrival tasks normally require successful boarding and arrival within 7 of the destination. Swim-to-boat tasks instead end near the stern platform, while boarding tasks require the boarding transition itself. Shore-arrival tasks require grounded walking on land, above the water surface, within 2.5 of the endpoint. The beaching variant additionally checks that the boat is grounded and its full footprint is on land. Shore-to-platform transport-choice variants accept surface arrival by swimming or boat. The submarine variant requires crossing the pipe mouth and reaching its interior goal section with valid depth, alignment, and hull clearance. Aerial. The agent must board the aircraft, take off, satisfy the configured aerial objective, and land at the designated recovery site. Flight waypoints are ordered three-dimensional gates, with radii of 65 for planes and 16 for helicopters. Approach objectives require coming within 60 of the moving aircraft; hover objectives require three continuous seconds within 12 of the target at speed no greater than 3 m/s. Landing requires ground contact at the correct runway or helipad after recorded takeoff and landing, speed at most 1.5 m/s, throttle below 5%, and two continuous seconds stopped. Helicopters must also be within 12 of the designated landing point. Crashing, exiting the task aircraft, or leaving the allowed flight region causes failure. An aircraft-approach task also fails if the target leaves its task airspace before the approach condition is met. Shooting and Sniping. The evaluator transforms the reticles impact point back into the annotated image coordinate system, accounting for camera movement and scope magnification. Ordinary shooting tests the annotated target box and any required target-part mask; sniping tests the corresponding target polygons. In both cases, exclusion regions are removed from the accepted hit region, and head-specific tasks use the annotated head region. Single-target shooting and sniping allow one shot: hit succeeds and miss fails. In multi-target sniping, task with 𝐾 targets supplies exactly 𝐾 bullets and requires 𝐾 distinct valid hits. An unscoped shot, miss, or repeated hit on an already cleared target immediately fails multi-target task. Single-target sniping uses seeded dispersion for unscoped fire where supported, while scoped fire uses point impact. 15 Interaction budgets and termination precedence. Online episodes allow up to 300 interaction rounds, and image-based tasks allow up to 20. Exhausting the round budget without success yields zero credit. Following requires the agent to maintain the required proximity until the NPC reaches its endpoint. Task-specific failures, including capture, aircraft destruction, and the target reaching its endpoint in Interception, take precedence over completion. A.3 Agent Action Space The agent controls the environment through shared keyboardmouse interface. Each response specifies one action object with required keys array and an optional mouse object. Keyboard entries pair key with its hold duration; mouse entries specify movement, scrolling, or button state changes. The conventional GUI agent emits this object as JSON text; the harness agent places it in game_step.action, alongside unique request_id. Table 4 summarizes the interface. Field keys mouse.move mouse.scroll mouse.buttons wait_seconds Parameters List of key and duration_seconds pairs Relative pixel displacement (𝑑𝑥 , 𝑑𝑦) Direction (up/down), integer steps 16 Left/right button with down/up event Timed wait with an empty keyboard array Table 4 Model-facing action schema. Mouse movement and scrolling are mutually exclusive within response; button events may accompany either. Keyboard inputs. The permitted keys are w, a, s, d, Shift, Control, Space, e, f, q, c, v, g, and Numpad4/5/6/8. Uppercase single-letter inputs and Ctrl are normalized to their canonical names. Each key appears at most once per response and has finite duration 𝑑 (0, 𝑑max], with default limit of 𝑑max = 1 second. For native 3D tasks, the duration is rounded upward to simulation frames at 60 Hz, and all specified keys start together or continue an existing hold. Keys are released independently as their durations expire; the turn duration is the maximum scheduled hold duration rather than their sum. There is no within-turn sequence of delayed key presses. Mouse inputs. All observations use 1280 720 viewport. Mouse movement uses relative pixel displacement, with 640 𝑑𝑥 640 and 360 𝑑𝑦 360; finite fractional values are permitted. Positive 𝑑𝑥 looks right and positive 𝑑𝑦 looks up. Repeating nonzero displacement changes the current view again. The aiming center in shooting and sniping remains at (640, 360); native 3D tasks apply camera sensitivity rather than guaranteeing exact centering of an image point. The agent can also scroll up or down by one to six steps, or issue down/up events for the left and right buttons, with at most one event per button in turn. Mouse inputs have no duration parameter and do not advance simulated time. In native 3D tasks, keys held through the end of turn remain held while inference Persistent input state. is paused. Including the same key in the next response continues the hold; omitting it releases it before simulation resumes. Mouse buttons remain in their current state until an explicit release or episode cleanup. View orientation persists across turns, and no cursor coordinate is supplied as additional observation text. An empty keys array releases previous keyboard holds. With no mouse operation or wait, this produces zero-time no-op that still consumes an interaction step. The optional wait_seconds field accepts finite duration in (0, 1] seconds with keys:[]. Instantaneous mouse operations occur first, then the simulation advances for the requested wait; image-based tasks consume turn without advancing scene time. All held inputs are released when an episode ends. 16 Example. The following native action first applies relative mouse movement of 120 pixels right and 30 pixels up, then holds for one second and Space for 0.1 seconds concurrently. The scheduled turn duration is one second, and the next screenshot is returned after execution or earlier task termination. { } "keys": [ {"key": "w", "duration_seconds": 1}, {"key": "Space", "duration_seconds": 0.1} ], "mouse": {"move": {"dx": 120, "dy": 30}} Image-based aiming tasks. Shooting and sniping use the mouse portion of the same schema; agents are instructed to submit an empty keyboard array, and well-formed keyboard inputs are ignored by the executor. Ordinary shooting supports aiming movement and left-button down to fire. Sniping additionally supports right-button down/up for scope control, left-button up, and scrolling to adjust magnification. Each scroll step maps to 160 ms of the aiming engines zoom operation, without advancing simulation clock. shot terminates single-target task; multi-target sniping continues until all targets are cleared or failure occurs, as specified in Appendix A.2. Each response consumes one of the twenty available interaction steps. The prompt requests one aiming operation per turn; the current executor also accepts composite mouse inputs without an intermediate observation. Validation. Each action object is validated before execution. Unknown fields, duplicate keys or buttons, invalid durations, out-of-range mouse displacements, simultaneous movement and scrolling, and waiting with nonempty keyboard array are rejected. For conventional GUI responses, the parser also accepts single JSON code block enclosing the entire response, without surrounding explanation, although the prompt requests plain JSON. Unpaused game time includes simulation advance during inference. A.4 Model Configurations Table 6 lists the reasoning effort settings used for the results in Table 2 and Figures 1 and 3. These resolved values identify the concrete instance; the input ranges describe the family of instances from which it was sampled. B.1 On-Foot RL Training Setup Generated training split. We use generation seed 20261027 to construct 50 on-foot instances. Route lengths and turn counts follow the empirical joint distribution of the 16 benchmark on-foot tasks, with 5% length tolerance for new routes. The resulting routes span 88.9131.4 meters and zero to four turns; 19 instances include destination landmarks such as motorcycles, sedans, vans, or convertibles. The generator checks route feasibility using the movement controller and enforces spatial separation from the benchmark on-foot routes. Training and evaluation use distinct task instances within the same city and controllers. Optimization and interaction. We train rank-32 LoRA adapters with 𝛼 = 64 on the language models attention query and value projections; the vision encoder and base model weights remain frozen. GRPO uses AdamW with constant learning rate of 106 and clipping ratio 0.2. Each update uses four tasks and eight rollouts per task, collecting 32 concurrent trajectories; optimization uses eight H200 GPUs. Training uses the native Codex history and automatic compaction, the same game rules. Instructions appear in the initial screenshot, and inference pauses the environment. The context window is 1M tokens, generation is capped at 32,768 tokens per response, actions at one second, and episodes at 300 interaction rounds. B.2 Reward Implementation Details We detail the terminal reward defined in Eq. 2 for the on-foot GRPO experiment. 20 Normalized distance progress. Let 𝑃(𝜏) denote the clipped fractional distance reduction in Eq. 2. Normalization makes equal fractional reductions comparable across route lengths. Moving farther from the destination yields zero progress, and revisiting locations provides no accumulated bonus: only the final distance is used. The factor (1 𝑆) applies the distance bonus only to unsuccessful rollouts. Thus successful rollout receives either 1 or 0.9, while an unsuccessful rollout receives at most 0.3. Traversable-distance measurement. Distances are approximated on one-meter, eight-neighbor walking grid using A* search with the environments collision and surface-height checks. The search is independent of the displayed purple route and permits physically feasible shortcuts. An unreachable or unsupported-height final position receives 𝑃 = 0. Distance computation failures are treated as invalid reward evidence, not as zero task progress. These measurements are host-side training signals and are not included in the agents observations. Round penalty and terminal scoring. The 0.1 deduction is applied once when 𝑁 > 100; it is not charged per additional round and is not applied at exactly 100 rounds. 𝑁 includes executed-action rounds and feedback rounds that resume an unfinished agent after premature final response. The reward is assigned once at the end of the rollout, with no intermediate distance rewards. An unsuccessful rollout ending at game-time or interaction limit retains its final-distance progress term. Benchmark evaluation continues to report binary task success alone.
